text: You're given an array of positive integers, nums, and a positive target. Return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target. If there's no such subarray, return zero.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — every number is positive, and that's the key property here. For target seven and the array two, three, one, two, four, three, the answer is two, from the subarray four, three. And if the whole array sums below target, I return zero. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Right. n is up to ten to the fifth, and target is up to ten to the ninth.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every start and extend to the right until the sum reaches target. That's quadratic, too slow for a hundred thousand numbers. This problem reminds me of a variable-length sliding window, the shortest flavor. I grow r and add to a running total; as soon as the total reaches target, I shrink from the left as far as I can, recording the length each time it's still feasible. It mirrors the longest flavor: longest shrinks while the window is invalid, shortest shrinks while it's valid. One thing worth flagging — positivity is what makes this work. Shrinking always lowers the sum, so the decision to shrink is monotone. With negatives this breaks, and I'd need prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead.
The follow-up also asks for an n log n solution.

Since every number is positive, prefix sums are strictly increasing. So for each right end, I can binary-search the rightmost left end that still gives a sum of at least target. That's n log n. I'll show it after the linear one.

Here's the plan. One: start with total at zero, the best length at infinity, and l at zero. Two: for each r, add the number at r to the total. Three: while the total is at least target, record the length first, then subtract the number at l and move l right. At the end, if the best length never changed, return zero. The order inside the loop matters: record before shrinking, because the current feasible window may be the shortest. This is linear time and constant space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Go ahead and code it.

Alright, let me code this up. The right pointer adds each number to total. Then a while loop shrinks: record r minus l plus one, subtract the left number, and move l. At the end, if min L is still the max int, nothing ever reached target, so I return zero. One thing worth flagging — the shrink has to be a while, not an if. One new big number can make the window feasible across several left steps, and an if would shrink only once and miss the shorter windows. For the follow-up, I build the prefix array, and for each r, upper bound finds the first prefix greater than pre r minus target. The one just before it is the rightmost valid left end.

Let's dry-run the code. Target seven, array two, three, one, two, four, three — expected two. The row that matters is the last one: adding three makes the total nine. The window still holds at length three, so I record three and drop the two. The total is seven, still feasible, so I record two and drop the four. Now the total is three, below target, and min L ends at two, from four, three. That matches. Corner case: if the sum of everything is below target, the while loop never runs, min L stays at the max int, and I return zero.
Why record before shrinking, not after?

Because the current feasible window might be the shortest one. Removing one more element might drop the sum below target, and that shorter window isn't valid. If I only measured after removing an element, I'd miss the real answer.

Let me think about complexity here. The sliding window is linear time and constant space. Even with the inner while loop, l only moves forward, at most n times in total, so the work is amortized linear. The prefix sum version is n log n time and linear space. Oh, one more thing — the same shrink-while-valid template also finds the shortest window covering a set of characters; only the validity check changes. And if negatives are allowed, I'd switch to a monotonic deque over prefix sums.
Great. Shrink while valid, record before shrinking, knowing why positivity matters, and both the linear and the n log n solutions. Good work.
